overview.title: 📖 Overview: Placement, Sanctity, and the Mechanics of the Mitzva
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 22a–22b
overview.hebrewSource: הַדְלָקָה עוֹשָׂה מִצְוָה, אוֹ הַנָּחָה עוֹשָׂה מִצְוָה?
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens with the rule that a Chanukah lamp placed above twenty cubits is invalid, like a sukka roof or an alleyway beam beyond that height — people simply don't look up that far. A drash on Joseph's pit follows on the heels of the same chain of tradents. The Gemara then works out exactly where the lamp goes (within a handbreadth of the door, on the left so it and the mezuza flank the entrant), whether the lamp carries enough sanctity to forbid using its light for mundane purposes like counting coins, and a three-way dispute between Rav and Shmuel about lighting one Chanukah lamp from another. That last question opens onto the daf's central theoretical puzzle, tested against the Temple candelabrum: does the act of lighting accomplish the mitzva, or does setting the lit lamp in its proper place?

slides.title: 📏 Not Above Twenty Cubits
slides.text: A Chanukah lamp placed higher than twenty cubits is invalid — the same standard as an invalid sukka roof or an alleyway's symbolic beam, since people do not ordinarily raise their eyes above that height. In the same chain of transmission (Rav Kahana citing Rav Natan bar Manyumi in the name of Rav Tanchum), the Gemara adds an unrelated drash on Joseph's pit: וְהַבּוֹר רֵק אֵין בּוֹ מָיִם — 'the pit was empty, there was no water in it.' Since 'empty' already implies no water, the extra words teach: no water, but snakes and scorpions were in it.
slides.hebrewSource: וְהַבּוֹר רֵק אֵין בּוֹ מָיִם — מַיִם אֵין בּוֹ, אֲבָל נְחָשִׁים וְעַקְרַבִּים יֵשׁ בּוֹ

slides.title: 🚪 Precise Placement of the Chanukah Lamp
slides.subtitle: Within a handbreadth of the door — but which side?
rows: Within the handbreadth immediately adjacent to the entrance
Left — so the Chanukah lamp is on the left and the mezuza on the right, surrounding the one entering with mitzvot

slides.title: 💰 Does the Chanukah Lamp Have Sanctity?
slides.subtitle: Shmuel questions Rav's ruling; Rav Yosef defends it by analogy

lines.speaker: Rav
lines.text: It is forbidden to count money by the light of the Chanukah lamp.

lines.speaker: Shmuel
lines.text: Does the Chanukah lamp have sanctity, that using its light should be forbidden?

lines.speaker: R' Yosef
lines.text: Does the blood of a slaughtered animal have sanctity? Yet the baraita on covering blood teaches: don't cover it with your foot — so that mitzvot are not treated with contempt. Here too, that principle applies.

lines.speaker: Query
lines.text: What about using sukka decorations during the seven days of the festival?

lines.speaker: R' Yosef
lines.text: That's a poor comparison — sukka decorations are explicitly forbidden in a baraita; the Chanukah lamp is not. The real paradigm for both is the blood-covering law.

callout.label: Underlying idea:
callout.text: Even without formal sanctity, an object of a mitzva may not be casually repurposed — 'so that mitzvot are not treated with contempt' (shelo yehu mitzvot bezuyot alav).

slides.title: 🕯️ Three Disputes Where Rabba Follows Shmuel
slides.subtitle: Abaye's summary: usually Rav, but not here

boxes.title: Rav's View: Forbidden
items: May not light one Chanukah lamp directly from another
May not untie tzitzit strings from one garment to move them to another
Halakha does NOT follow Rabbi Shimon's lenient view on dragging (gerira)

boxes.title: Shmuel's View: Permitted
items: May move tzitzit strings between garments
Halakha DOES follow Rabbi Shimon on dragging — a bed, chair, or bench may be dragged if a furrow is not intended

callout.label: Abaye's report:
callout.text: In every other matter Rabba ruled like Rav — except these three, where he ruled like Shmuel. The reason for Rav's lamp-to-lamp ban is disputed: contempt for the mitzva, or 'weakening' it by using its oil for another task.

slides.title: 🤔 Lighting or Placing — Which Accomplishes the Mitzva?
slides.subtitle: Tested against the Temple menorah's western lamp

nodes.content: ❓ Dilemma: does lighting the lamp fulfill the mitzva, or does placing the already-lit lamp in position fulfill it?
🕎 Objection from the Temple menorah's western lamp: since the lamps were fixed in place, priests had no choice but to light lamp-to-lamp with a wood chip — a problem either way

columns.label: Rav Pappa
columns.content: Answers: the wicks were long enough to reach directly, lamp to lamp — no wood chip needed

columns.label: Still difficult
columns.content: For the view that lamp-to-lamp 'weakens the mitzva,' the question remains unresolved: קַשְׁיָא

nodes.content: ✅ Rav Huna son of Rabbi Yehoshua's rule: if lighting accomplishes the mitzva, one may light lamp-to-lamp; if placing does, one may not

callout.label: Rava's proofs (examined next):
callout.text: Holding a lit lamp in one's hand accomplishes nothing (suggesting placing matters) — but this is explained away: onlookers assume he's just holding it for his own use, not yet performing the mitzva.

summary.principle: Precision in placing the Chanukah lamp — its height, its position at the door, and even whether it may be repurposed for mundane use — all trace back to one unresolved theoretical question: does the mitzva reside in the act of kindling, or in setting the lit lamp in its proper place?

flowSteps.content: 📏 A lamp above 20 cubits is invalid; placement rules follow: within a handbreadth of the door, on the left
💰 Shmuel questions the lamp's 'sanctity'; Rav Yosef defends the prohibition via the blood-covering analogy

columns.content: 🕯️ Rav forbids lighting lamp-to-lamp; Shmuel permits — Rabba follows Shmuel
🕎 Temple menorah tests the theory and leaves it unresolved for one view

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: whether hadlaka (lighting) or hanacha (placement) 'accomplishes' the mitzva determines a whole cluster of practical rulings

quiz.q: Why is a Chanukah lamp placed above twenty cubits invalid?
o: Because oil burns poorly at that height
Because, like an invalid sukka roof or alleyway beam, people do not ordinarily raise their eyes above twenty cubits
Because Roman law forbade it
Because the mishna requires the lamp to be at eye level exactly
quiz.e: The Gemara compares the twenty-cubit limit to the identical standard for a sukka's roofing and an alleyway's symbolic beam — objects above that height are not usually noticed.

quiz.q: According to the halakha reached on this daf, on which side of the doorway should the Chanukah lamp be placed?
o: On the right, opposite the mezuza
On the left, so the lamp and the mezuza flank the person entering
Directly above the doorway
Wherever is most convenient
quiz.e: The accepted halakha follows Rav Shmuel of Difti: place the lamp on the left, with the mezuza on the right, so that a person entering is surrounded by mitzvot.

quiz.q: How does Rav Yosef defend the ruling that one may not count money by the light of the Chanukah lamp, against Shmuel's objection that the lamp has no sanctity?
o: By citing an explicit verse forbidding it
By comparing it to the law of covering the blood of a slaughtered animal, which also lacks formal sanctity but may not be treated with contempt
By arguing the Chanukah lamp is fully consecrated like Temple vessels
He concedes Shmuel is correct
quiz.e: Rav Yosef argues from the blood-covering law — an act that, though the blood has no sanctity, must not be done disrespectfully — establishing the principle that mitzva objects should not be treated with contempt even without formal sanctity.

quiz.q: According to Abaye's summary, in how many matters did Rabba rule like Shmuel rather than like Rav, and what are they?
o: Two: lighting lamp-to-lamp and tzitzit only
Three: lighting lamp-to-lamp, moving tzitzit between garments, and the law of dragging (gerira) per Rabbi Shimon
Four, including a ruling about sukka decorations
None — Rabba always followed Rav
quiz.e: Abaye reports that in all other matters Rabba followed Rav, except these three: lighting from lamp to lamp, untying tzitzit from one garment to another, and following Rabbi Shimon's lenient ruling on dragging.

quiz.q: What problem does the Temple menorah's western lamp raise for the dispute over whether lighting or placing accomplishes the Chanukah mitzva?
o: It proves placing always accomplishes the mitzva with no difficulty
Since the Temple lamps were fixed in place, priests seemingly had to light lamp-to-lamp, which is difficult for the view that this 'weakens' the mitzva
It has no bearing on the discussion at all
It proves that only priests may perform this mitzva
quiz.e: Since the menorah's lamps couldn't be removed to light one from another with direct contact, priests needed a wood chip or long wick to light lamp-to-lamp — creating a difficulty for the opinion that lighting one Chanukah lamp from another 'weakens' the mitzva, a difficulty the Gemara leaves unresolved (kashya).
